strengths: Well-motivated problem reformulation: Compelling argument that input video priors should be leveraged rather than discarded, addressing genuine limitations of noise-initialized diffusion models
Theoretically sound VP-SDE bridge formulation with rigorous boundary conditions and velocity-matching training objective that avoids expensive SDE simulation
Elegant adaptive mask modulation (AMM) strategy that addresses the background-fidelity vs. generative-flexibility trade-off through simple but effective feature amplification
Thoughtful dataset construction combining synthetic ROSE data with real-world compositions using SAM2 and Qwen3-VL filtering, with acknowledged limitations mitigation
Interesting emergent capability of implicit shadow removal even without explicit masks, suggesting effective contextual understanding
Clear presentation and motivation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) and well-organized sections
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation. No LPIPS, SSIM, FVD, or temporal consistency metrics provided despite central claims of 'significant outperformance'. Impossible to objectively verify performance without metrics

No ablation studies to validate design choices: (1) Bridge vs. standard diffusion comparison missing, (2) AMM isolated contribution not demonstrated, (3) variance schedule sensitivity not analyzed, (4) impact of Wan2.1-1.3B initialization unclear

Insufficient technical specifications harm reproducibility: guidance term h(zt,t,zsrc) derivation omitted, SDE solver weights w1,w2,w3 computation unspecified ('analytically determined' is vague), VAE details missing, variance schedule parameterization unclear

No systematic failure analysis despite identifying that strong priors hinder large object removal. Missing quantitative characterization of mask-size sensitivity, failure case examples, and applicability guidance

Dual-role conditioning of zsrc (as prior and spatial condition) lacks justification. Why is this better than alternatives? Doesn't this provide excessive information twice? Could simpler approaches work?

Dataset construction concerns: (1) Composition-based synthetic data may create domain gaps with natural videos, (2) Qwen3-VL filtering mechanism under-specified with no rejection rate statistics, (3) ROSE bias claims lack quantitative evidence, (4) potential data leakage risk not discussed

Large pre-training initialization from Wan2.1-1.3B raises fairness concerns. Unclear how much improvement comes from bridge formulation vs. foundation model. No random initialization baseline provided

Incomplete experimental setup: baseline comparison fairness unclear (resolution, inference steps, computational budget), temporal consistency shown qualitatively only, text conditioning contribution not analyzed, generalization to complex/extreme scenarios not tested

Missing implementation details: batch size, gradient accumulation, mixed precision, VAE compression ratio, training convergence analysis, inference time comparison with baselines, hyperparameter sensitivity
Reproducibility deficits: code release not mentioned, custom composite dataset availability unclear, hyperparameters scattered throughout, Algorithm 1 lacks crucial training specifics

strengths: Sound mathematical framework: The VP-SDE bridge formulation is properly derived and theoretically grounded in existing bridge model theory
Well-motivated approach: Reformulating video inpainting as video-to-video translation with a data-to-data prior is intuitive and addresses real limitations of noise-initialized methods
Clever dual-role conditioning: Using source latent zsrc as both the bridge prior and spatial condition is an elegant design choice
Comprehensive data curation: Combining 16K synthetic samples (ROSE) with 31K real-world composite samples demonstrates effort to improve generalization
Clear presentation: Introduction and methodology sections are well-written with good motivation for the paradigm shift from noise-to-data to data-to-data
Visually competitive results: Qualitative examples suggest the method produces reasonable visual quality and temporal coherence
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation - No LPIPS, SSIM, FID, temporal consistency metrics, or any numerical results. All comparisons are purely visual assessment. This alone is disqualifying for a top-tier venue like ICML

No ablation studies - Cannot verify the contribution of individual components, especially the main claimed contribution (AMM). No bridge vs. standard diffusion baseline. Essential for validating design choices
Incomplete experiments section - Section 5 jumps from setup to qualitative results, entirely omitting quantitative evaluation, ablations, efficiency analysis, failure modes, and user studies

Oversimplified AMM mechanism - Equation 15 is merely a learnable scalar multiplier on background features. Lacks rigorous justification and empirical validation. Not a substantial technical contribution

Limited and incomplete baseline comparisons - Only 3 methods compared; missing DiffuEraser (Li et al., 2025b), the most relevant recent concurrent work. No comparison with standard diffusion-based inpainting

Questionable data construction - Custom dataset uses composition-based approach (SAM2 + background blending). Potential for synthetic artifacts not discussed. Qwen3-VL filtering procedure vaguely described and not validated. No domain gap analysis

Incremental novelty - Straightforward application of existing bridge models (Liu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023a) to video inpainting. FrameBridge (Wang et al., 2025) already extended bridges to I2V synthesis

Missing critical technical details - Derivation of velocity target (Eq. 11) deferred to appendix. SDE solver weights (w1, w2, w3) claimed analytically determined but not derived. Hyperparameter choices (βmin, βmax) not justified or analyzed
Inadequate reproducibility - No code release promised. Custom dataset creation incompletely specified. Qwen3-VL filtering procedure not reproducible. Computational requirements not quantified
No efficiency analysis - No inference time, memory usage, or computational cost comparisons with baselines. Total training cost (20K steps × 8 H100s) not reported
Missing failure case analysis - No discussion of when and why the method fails, or limitations of the bridge formulation for this task
Unsupported claims - Statements like 'significantly outperforms' and 'implicit shadow removal' lack quantitative evidence and are difficult to verify from visual inspection

strengths: Well-motivated paradigm shift from noise-to-data to data-to-data generation for video inpainting, addressing real limitations of existing diffusion-based approaches
Technically sound VP-SDE bridge formulation with rigorous velocity-matching objective (Eq. 11-12) and proper mathematical grounding
Novel Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) strategy provides practical solution to balance background fidelity with generative flexibility for varying occlusion sizes
Strong qualitative results demonstrating superior texture quality and temporal consistency; interesting emergent property of implicit shadow removal without explicit supervision
Thoughtful dataset construction combining synthetic (ROSE) and 31,000 real-world composite samples with distribution bias mitigation
Clear presentation with well-structured methodology, proper algorithms, and good visual comparisons across diverse scenarios
weaknesses: Critical absence of quantitative evaluation: no LPIPS, SSIM, FVD, or temporal consistency metrics provided, making rigorous validation impossible and enabling potential selection bias in qualitative examples
No ablation studies validating key design choices: AMM necessity, VP-SDE vs. Brownian Bridge, dual conditioning benefits, variance schedule sensitivity, or component contributions to improvements
Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing bridge model techniques (Zhou et al., 2023a; Chen et al., 2023) to new domain; AMM is relatively simple element-wise modulation
Incomplete experimental scope: no user studies, failure case analysis, computational efficiency comparison, performance across object scales, or systematic resolution sensitivity analysis

Reproducibility concerns: no code release, vague SAM2/Qwen3-VL filtering details, unjustified hyperparameters (β_min=0.01, β_max=50.0, 1000 timesteps, 50 inference steps), missing variance schedule specification and architecture modifications

Mathematical clarity gaps: guidance term h(z_t,t,z_src) tractability claimed but not proven; relationship between β(t) and σ_t scheduling unclear; AMM's mathematical interaction with bridge dynamics not analyzed
Lack of failure mode discussion: while paper acknowledges strong priors hinder large object removal, no empirical validation, systematic analysis, or discussion of when/why this occurs

strengths: Technically sound framework with rigorous mathematical foundation: VP-SDE bridge formulation is theoretically grounded with complete derivations of marginal distributions and training equivalence to score matching (Appendix B)

Strong comprehensive experimental validation: Achieves best or second-best results across all metrics on both DAVIS and new BridgeRemoval-Bench; 1.64 dB PSNR improvement demonstrates clear advance; user study with 1,440 evaluations from 24 participants provides independent validation

Addresses a real technical challenge: Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) elegantly resolves the trade-off between leveraging strong source priors (good for background preservation) and enabling sufficient deviation for large object removal, with clear ablation evidence
Practical efficiency: Achieves 1.111 s/frame inference—2-11x faster than most baselines while maintaining quality, making the approach practically deployable

Useful community contribution: BridgeRemoval-Bench provides diverse evaluation scenarios (150 videos across landscape/portrait, single/multiple objects, real/synthetic/in-the-wild) addressing limitations of DAVIS
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-organized paper with detailed algorithms, implementation specifics, and comprehensive appendices including mathematical proofs and design justifications
Novel application of bridge models to video object removal task, establishing this as a viable alternative to noise-to-data diffusion paradigm for video generation
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Primary contribution is applying existing DDBM framework (Zhou et al., 2023a) to a new domain; AMM is a relatively straightforward FiLM-based adaptation without significant algorithmic innovation

Insufficient theoretical insight: Paper lacks analysis of why data-to-data bridge paths specifically benefit video object removal versus general generative tasks; claims are primarily empirical rather than mechanistic

Underexplored design choices: AMM design rationale compares only with/without rather than exploring alternatives (e.g., cross-attention, residual scaling); variance schedule coefficients (βmin=0.01, βmax=50.0) not justified or ablated

Significant failure mode unaddressed: Fast-moving objects acknowledged as problematic but no solution attempted; limitation presented as general field challenge without systematic characterization of when/why the method fails

Reproducibility barriers: No code release plans mentioned; depends on closed-source models (SAM2, Qwen3-VL) and proprietary data sources; requires 8 H100 GPUs for training; likely to limit community adoption and verification
Benchmark scale modest: BridgeRemoval-Bench contains only 150 videos despite being positioned as comprehensive; unclear if training on 16,000 ROSE synthetic samples introduces bias toward that method

Metric limitations acknowledged but not addressed: VBench relegated to appendix with acknowledged low discriminative power; CLIP-T/F are proxy metrics not directly measuring removal quality; PSNR/MSE only computed on unmasked regions

Incomplete baseline analysis: Some baselines (Senoria, Ditto) from Feb 2025 arxiv; no controlled ablation comparing diffusion vs. bridge on identical architecture; VACE's trade-off (high PSNR, low CLIP-T) not thoroughly investigated

strengths: Well-motivated core idea of using source video as structural prior rather than random noise for video object removal
Rigorous mathematical foundation with correct derivations of VP-SDE bridge marginals and equivalence to score matching
Practical Adaptive Mask Modulation mechanism effectively addresses trade-off between background preservation and large object removal
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including new BridgeRemoval-Bench benchmark with 150 annotated videos across diverse scenarios
Strong quantitative results achieving best or second-best performance on most metrics (e.g., 1.64 dB PSNR improvement on new benchmark)
Solid user study with 1,440 evaluations demonstrating consistent preference across multiple criteria
Clear presentation with thorough related work, detailed algorithms, and ablation studies including inference step analysis
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Bridge models (Chen et al. 2021), VP-SDE (Song et al. 2021), and velocity-driven training are all well-established; applying them to video object removal is sensible but incremental

Critical missing ablation: No Flow Matching baseline with identical source video initialization to isolate whether improvements stem from the bridge formulation vs. simply having strong initialization

Unfair experimental comparisons: Different base models, potentially different training data volumes across methods, conflation of framework choice (VP-SDE vs. Flow Matching) with prior choice (source video)

Overstated core claim: Paper argues noise-to-data paradigm is 'suboptimal' but lacks rigorous theoretical justification beyond intuition; reference-guided diffusion methods partially address the same issue
Modest quantitative improvements: While best-performing, improvements are often marginal (CLIP-F: 0.9701→0.9768 on DAVIS, ~0.7% relative gain; CLIP-T consistently underperforms competitors)

Acknowledged limitation inadequately addressed: Substantial failures on fast-moving objects (Figure 6 shows visible artifacts); dismissing this as 'not specific to our approach' sidesteps practical concerns
Evaluation metric concerns: CLIP-T/F are proxy metrics not ground-truth measures; paper dismisses VBench as having 'limited discriminative power' but includes results in appendix (somewhat defensive)
Reproducibility issues: Model pre-training details vague, code availability not mentioned, project page URL missing, real-world composite dataset (31K videos) availability unclear
Missing critical analyses: Limited characterization of when bridge formulation helps most, no sensitivity analysis to variance schedule choices, insufficient exploration of hyperparameter impact
Insufficient ablation depth: AMM is FiLM-based modulation without strong novelty; limited analysis of alternative solutions to the large-object trade-off

strengths: Well-motivated reformulation from noise-to-data to data-to-data generation with clear intuition for video object removal domain
Rigorous mathematical foundation with proper derivation of VP-SDE bridge marginal distribution, analytical guidance term, and equivalence proofs to score matching

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including new BridgeRemoval-Bench benchmark (150 videos), 6 baseline comparisons, user study with 1,440 evaluations, and multiple metrics addressing both object removal and background preservation
Strong empirical results with 1.64 dB PSNR improvement on proposed benchmark and consistent best or second-best performance across all quantitative metrics
Practical solution to bridge-prior rigidity trade-off via Adaptive Mask Modulation that enables effective removal of objects across scales
Clear algorithmic presentation with detailed pseudo-code, good figures, and thorough ablation studies on key components
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: primarily applies established bridge theory (DDBM) to video inpainting domain; AMM is essentially standard FiLM conditioning applied to mask features
Adaptive Mask Modulation insufficiently explored: no comparative ablations against alternative modulation strategies; sensitivity to design choices and hyperparameters not analyzed
Incomplete ablation studies: missing investigation of dual-role of zsrc, variance schedule sensitivity, VAE/text encoder choices, and alternative conditioning mechanisms

Limited failure mode analysis: fast-moving objects acknowledged but not systematically investigated; no principled solutions proposed; missing statistics on failure frequency and other failure taxonomy

Evaluation methodology concerns: CLIP metrics as proxies not thoroughly validated; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals despite small metric differences; user study with modest sample size (24 participants)
Generalization questions: all experiments use single backbone (Wan2.1-1.3B); no cross-architecture validation; unclear how method-specific design choices are to this architecture

Training data analysis sparse: no ablation decomposing contribution of synthetic vs. real-world data; distribution characteristics of combined dataset not characterized; potential dataset biases unaddressed
Inference efficiency trade-off unexplained: 50% slower than ROSE baseline; no discussion of computational cost drivers or fine-grained inference speed analysis
Reproducibility gaps: project page URL incomplete; code release not mentioned; dataset sourcing details missing (especially TikTok permissions); Qwen3-VL filtering criteria not specified
Technical details under-explored: hyperparameter choices (variance schedule β values, learning rate) not justified; VAE latent quantization effects not discussed; sensitivity analysis absent
